summary:
San Marino criminalises neither same-sex conduct nor gender identity. Consensual same-sex acts were decriminalised in 1864; the residual Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which punished habitual homosexual acts causing public scandal with three months to one year of imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. No statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use.

Entry carries no documented friction. The land border with Italy is open, and no identity screening that would out an arriving trans visitor is recorded. A visitor's foreign documents govern identity throughout the stay.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing a gender marker. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers, since a visitor's documentation is not reissued locally.

Protection machinery covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. A 2008 amendment to the Penal Code outlawed discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation, effective 3 May 2008, and provides sentence enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Gender identity is absent from that provision. In November 2019 San Marino accepted recommendations from the UN Universal Periodic Review to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity; no implementing text is recorded.

The constitutional layer stops at sexual orientation. A referendum on 2 June 2019 added sexual orientation to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights with 71.46 per cent in favour, after a council vote in March 2019 fell short at 35 for, 8 against and 1 abstention against the 39 required.

Partner recognition exists but is narrower than marriage. Civil unions, in force from 5 December 2018 and fully operational from 11 February 2019, are open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and carry rights over residency, citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Same-sex couples remain barred from marrying, and households headed by same-sex couples do not receive the same legal protections as opposite-sex households. A December 2017 budget-law amendment that would allow foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism had no implementing legislation drafted as of 2024.

Violence against LGBTQ people is reported occasionally, without published figures that would allow comparison against the general crime rate.

Official representation has shifted: Paolo Rondelli's appointment as captain regent in 2022 made San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly gay head of state, on a six-month term carrying no executive power.
tangentialFactors:
The civil-unions statute was presented domestically as leaner than Italy's Cirinnà law, so the recognition available to a couple registered in San Marino is narrower than in the neighbouring framework.

The constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination arrived by referendum after the legislature failed to reach the required supermajority, which places the enacted protection ahead of the parliamentary consensus behind it.

How often the 2008 hate-crime enhancements are applied in practice is not documented in any source reviewed.
localsOnly:
Residents have no administrative or judicial route to change a gender marker, which affects identity documents, civil-union registration and any record that carries legal sex.

Civil unions give same-sex couples rights over residency, citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption, but marriage remains closed to them and same-sex-headed households are excluded from protections available to opposite-sex households.

Sex education and emotional education programmes expressly cover LGBTQ rights, and the curriculum of education to citizenship addresses the same ground.

Hate-crime sentence enhancements are available for bias based on sexual orientation only; gender identity has no equivalent statutory footing despite the 2019 acceptance of Universal Periodic Review recommendations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2026 ILGA Annual Review's legal gender recognition chapter does not cover San Marino; its documented cases concern Albania and Andorra.

No published statistics record the application of the 2008 hate-crime enhancements or the number of anti-LGBTQ incidents.

Article 274 was never reported as applied before its repeal.

Whether implementing legislation for the 2017 provision on foreign same-sex marriages has been drafted since 2024 is unresolved.
